questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: The octopus relies on its keen color vision to match the exact colors of its surroundings.
choices.rationale: The passage says the octopus is colorblind, not keen-sighted.

choices.text: The octopus changes color mainly to communicate with other nearby octopuses.
choices.rationale: Communication between octopuses is never mentioned.

choices.text: The octopus shifts color slowly, building up a disguise over many minutes.
choices.rationale: The change happens in under a second, not over many minutes.

choices.text: The octopus changes color through a muscular pigment system it cannot itself see.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage centers on the surprising mechanism of color change in a colorblind animal.

questions.explanation: The passage builds toward the paradox of an animal that produces colors it cannot perceive.

stimulus.title: The Color of Thought
stimulus.text: An octopus has no bones and, oddly, almost no color of its own. Yet in less than a second it can flush deep red with alarm or fade to match the speckled gray of a stone. Beneath its skin lie millions of tiny sacs of pigment, each ringed by muscle. When the muscles pull, the sacs widen and color blooms; when they relax, the color vanishes. Stranger still, the octopus is colorblind, so it cannot see the very hues it produces. Some researchers suspect its skin itself senses light, letting the animal paint a disguise it can never admire.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Maps drawn in earlier centuries in fact contained no errors of any kind.
choices.rationale: The passage describes early errors.

choices.text: Explorers of the period actually preferred to use inaccurate, guesswork maps.
choices.rationale: Explorers corrected maps; they did not prefer errors.

choices.text: Mapmakers of the past genuinely believed that sea monsters filled the unexplored oceans.
choices.rationale: The passage says monsters were decoration 'less from belief.'

choices.text: Accurate maps were achieved gradually, replacing guesses with hard-won measurements.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage traces the replacement of guesses by measurements and honors the effort behind it.

questions.explanation: The passage's point is the slow, effortful move from guesswork to accuracy.

stimulus.title: The Edge of the Map
stimulus.text: Old maps are full of guesses. Where knowledge ran out, mapmakers filled the blank spaces with mountains they had never seen and coastlines that bent the wrong way. Some added sea monsters, less from belief than from a need to decorate the unknown. As explorers returned with measurements, the guesses were slowly corrected, and the monsters swam off the page. But a finished, accurate map can hide how hard it was to make. Every clean line was once a question, settled only by someone willing to sail past the edge of what was known and come back with an answer.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Tomas writes the letters mainly to impress the friends in his new city.
choices.rationale: The letters are addressed home, not aimed at impressing new friends.

choices.text: Tomas mails the most honest of his three letters to his family at last.
choices.rationale: He keeps the letter folded in a drawer rather than mailing it.

choices.text: Tomas decides he no longer misses his hometown now that he has moved.
choices.rationale: The passage shows he does miss home, not that he stopped.

choices.text: Writing an unsent letter helps Tomas privately acknowledge his homesickness.
choices.rationale: Correct. The closing lines show the unsent writing let him admit his homesickness.

questions.explanation: The narrative resolves on writing as a way to admit feelings to himself.

stimulus.title: The Unsent Letter
stimulus.text: Tomas wrote the letter three times before he stopped trying to send it. In the first version he was cheerful, listing the small triumphs of his new city as if homesickness were a thing he had outgrown. In the second he was honest, and the page filled with everything he missed until it embarrassed him. The third version said almost nothing at all. He kept that one folded in a drawer. Months later he found it again and realized the words he could not send had still done their work: writing them had let him admit, if only to himself, how far from home he truly felt.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Seeds kept in the frozen vault lose the ability to sprout within about a year.
choices.rationale: The cold lets seeds sprout even after decades.

choices.text: A frozen seed vault preserves crop diversity as a backup against future losses.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains the vault as a rarely used backup that protects crop variety.

choices.text: The frozen seed vault is opened and drawn upon by its keepers nearly every single day.
choices.rationale: The keepers hope it is rarely needed.

choices.text: The mountain vault was built mainly to store bars of gold rather than seeds.
choices.rationale: It values seeds 'more than gold,' figuratively.

questions.explanation: The passage frames the vault as a safeguard for crop diversity.

stimulus.title: A Vault for Seeds
stimulus.text: Deep inside a frozen mountain, a vault holds something more valuable than gold: seeds. Hundreds of thousands of varieties of crops, gathered from around the world, rest in sealed packets at temperatures far below freezing. The cold slows the seeds' aging to a crawl, so that even after decades they can still sprout. The vault is a backup. If a war, flood, or disease wipes out a crop somewhere, a sample can be withdrawn and grown again. Its keepers hope it will rarely be needed, the way one hopes never to use a fire extinguisher. Its value lies precisely in being ready and almost never used.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Lighthouses stopped working and went dark once automation was introduced.
choices.rationale: The lights 'still shine,' more reliably than before.

choices.text: Modern lighthouses still need a keeper to climb the tower every night.
choices.rationale: Automation withdrew the keepers.

choices.text: Automation made lighthouses more reliable but ended the human role of the keeper.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage contrasts improved reliability with the loss of the human keeper.

choices.text: Lighthouse keepers were never really necessary for the lights to function properly.
choices.rationale: Keepers performed essential tasks for centuries.

questions.explanation: The passage balances technical gain against a human loss.

stimulus.title: Keeping the Light
stimulus.text: For centuries, a lighthouse meant a keeper. Someone had to climb the tower each night, trim the wick, polish the lens, and wind the clockwork that turned the light. Storms made the work dangerous, and isolation made it lonely, but ships depended on that faithful beam. In the twentieth century, automation arrived. Electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors took over the tasks one by one, and keepers were gradually withdrawn. The lights still shine, more reliably than ever, yet something human slipped away with the last keeper. The machines kept the promise of the light; they could not keep its company.

questions.prompt: Which choice best captures the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: A fine instrument reveals the skill Nadia had built through her earlier struggle.
choices.rationale: Correct. The closing lines tie the fine violin to the skill she had quietly built.

choices.text: Nadia's teacher refuses to let her borrow the fine loaner violin at all.
choices.rationale: The teacher hands her the loaner rather than refusing.

choices.text: Nadia decides to give up the violin entirely once the recital has ended.
choices.rationale: She does not quit; she gains insight.

choices.text: Battered school instruments teach a student more than fine instruments ever could.
choices.rationale: The passage shows the loaner as finer than her battered school violin.

questions.explanation: The narrative resolves on the idea that her growth, not just the violin, produced the beautiful playing.

stimulus.title: The Borrowed Violin
stimulus.text: Nadia had practiced on a school instrument so battered that two of its pegs slipped during every lesson. When her teacher handed her a loaner violin for the recital, she nearly refused; it felt wrong to play something so fine. But as she drew the bow across the strings, the tone opened like a window onto a bright street. Notes she had fought for all year now arrived easily, as if the instrument had been waiting for her. Afterward, returning it to its case, she understood that her old struggles had not been wasted. The fine violin had simply revealed the player she had quietly become.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Glass loses a noticeable amount of its quality each time it is recycled again.
choices.rationale: The passage says glass keeps its quality when remade.

choices.text: Glass is endlessly recyclable in principle, but flawed systems keep much of it from reuse.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage contrasts glass's ideal recyclability with system failures.

choices.text: Glass, unlike most materials, simply cannot be recycled by any method at all.
choices.rationale: It says glass can be remade again and again.

choices.text: Sorting glass by color is the one step that actually makes recycling glass impossible to do.
choices.rationale: Color sorting is offered as a solution, not an obstacle to recycling.

questions.explanation: The passage's point is the gap between glass's ideal recyclability and imperfect systems.

stimulus.title: The Endless Material
stimulus.text: Glass has a quiet superpower: it can be melted down and remade again and again without losing quality. A bottle recycled today can become a bottle next month, then another after that, in a loop that, in principle, never wears out. Compared with this ideal, reality lags. Much glass still ends up in landfills because collection is uneven and because mixing colors lowers the value of the recycled material. Sorting by color and keeping glass out of general trash would let more of it re-enter the loop. The material is willing; it is our systems, the author suggests, that need redesigning.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Plain-looking salt marshes provide valuable protection that was long overlooked.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage shows the drab marsh doing protective work long unappreciated.

choices.text: Salt marshes are beautiful landscapes that people have always admired for their scenery.
choices.rationale: The passage calls the marsh drab and once-overlooked, not always admired.

choices.text: Salt marshes release large amounts of stored carbon into the warming air.
choices.rationale: The roots store carbon rather than releasing it.

choices.text: Draining marshes is the most effective way to defend homes from storms.
choices.rationale: Draining marshes removed protection rather than providing it.

questions.explanation: The passage reveals the overlooked marsh as a valuable natural protector.

stimulus.title: The Quiet Buffer
stimulus.text: Where the land meets the sea, a salt marsh can look like wasteland: flat, muddy, and crossed by winding channels. Yet this drab landscape does remarkable work. Its dense grasses slow incoming waves, blunting the force of storms before they reach homes inland. The same grasses trap sediment, letting the marsh build itself upward as the sea slowly rises. Beneath the mud, roots store carbon that might otherwise warm the air. For years, marshes were drained and filled without much thought. Only later did people recognize that the unglamorous marsh had been protecting them all along, asking nothing in return.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Bats can detect only objects that are holding completely still, never ones that are moving.
choices.rationale: Bats detect motion through shifts in the returning sound.

choices.text: Bats rely chiefly on their sharp eyesight to hunt insects after dark.
choices.rationale: The passage describes hunting by sound, not eyesight.

choices.text: Bats produce sounds that humans can easily hear during the night.
choices.rationale: The calls are often too high for humans to hear.

choices.text: Bats perceive their surroundings in the dark by interpreting echoes of their own calls.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how bats build a sound-based picture from echoes.

questions.explanation: The passage centers on echolocation as a sound-built perception of the world.

stimulus.title: Seeing With Sound
stimulus.text: A bat hunting in pitch darkness does not bump into things. It calls out, often at pitches too high for humans to hear, and listens for the echoes that bounce back. From the delay between call and echo, the bat judges how far away an object is; from subtle shifts in the returning sound, it can tell whether the object is moving toward it or away. A moth's fluttering wing returns a different echo than a still leaf. So precise is this sense that some bats can snatch an insect from the air in total darkness. The world the bat perceives is built entirely of sound, a picture painted with echoes.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Honeybees locate rich patches of flowers almost entirely by chance and luck.
choices.rationale: The dance communicates location, not luck.

choices.text: Honeybees actually speak to one another inside the hive using a range of distinct vocal sounds.
choices.rationale: The passage stresses communication 'without sound.'

choices.text: The honeybee's waggle dance is a symbolic code for a food source's direction and distance.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how the dance encodes direction and distance.

choices.text: The honeybee's waggle dance carries no consistent or reliable meaning at all.
choices.rationale: The dance reliably encodes specific information.

questions.explanation: The passage frames the waggle dance as a precise symbolic language.

stimulus.title: Dances in the Dark
stimulus.text: A foraging honeybee that finds a rich patch of flowers cannot simply tell the hive where to go. Instead, it dances. On the vertical comb, in darkness, the bee runs a straight line while waggling its body, then loops back to repeat the move. The angle of that straight run, measured against the pull of gravity, encodes the direction of the flowers relative to the sun. The length of the run signals distance. Watching bees crowd around and follow, researchers realized they were seeing a kind of symbolic language, one that passes precise information without sight, sound, or a single spoken word.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Fog nets can completely replace every other source of water in any location.
choices.rationale: The passage calls it a supplement, not a universal replacement.

choices.text: Harvesting water from fog demands complex machinery and a steady supply of electrical power.
choices.rationale: It relies on gravity and simple mesh, not complex machinery.

choices.text: Fog nets can supply useful drinking water in suitable coastal areas, within real limits.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage presents fog harvesting as useful where conditions fit, while noting limits.

choices.text: Fog almost never holds enough moisture to be worth trying to collect at all.
choices.rationale: The passage says nets can collect many liters.

questions.explanation: The balanced claim is that fog nets work well in the right setting but are not a cure-all.

stimulus.title: Catching Water From Air
stimulus.text: In a few dry coastal regions, drinking water can be harvested from fog. Tall mesh nets are strung across hillsides where moist air rolls in from the sea. As the fog drifts through, droplets cling to the mesh, merge, and trickle down into troughs and storage tanks. A single large net can collect many liters on a good day, enough to supplement a village's supply. The method is not a cure-all: it works only where fog is frequent and winds are steady, and the nets need upkeep. Yet in the right place, it turns a passing cloud into a dependable resource, using little more than gravity and patience.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Giant kelp grows so slowly that it can take many years to reach the surface.
choices.rationale: The passage says kelp grows astonishingly fast, not slowly.

choices.text: Sea otters are harmful pests that destroy the kelp forests they live in.
choices.rationale: Otters protect the kelp; their loss lets urchins destroy it.

choices.text: Kelp forests are rich but fragile habitats that depend on a balance of species.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage presents kelp forests as rich habitats whose health rests on species balance.

choices.text: Kelp forests are found mainly in warm, sandy waters near tropical beaches.
choices.rationale: The passage places these forests off cool, rocky coasts.

questions.explanation: The passage frames kelp forests as productive yet fragile, balanced ecosystems.

stimulus.title: Forests Beneath the Waves
stimulus.text: Off some cool, rocky coasts grow forests that no hiker will ever walk through. Giant kelp, anchored to the seafloor, can stretch dozens of meters toward the surface, swaying in the current like trees in wind. These kelp forests shelter fish, snails, and otters, much as a woodland shelters birds and deer. The kelp grows astonishingly fast, sometimes half a meter in a single day, drinking sunlight near the surface. But the forest is fragile. Where otters vanish, sea urchins multiply and graze the kelp down to bare rock, leaving a barren the divers call an urchin desert. A single missing animal can unmake a whole forest.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Coral grows faster than trees and so makes a more accurate calendar.
choices.rationale: The passage compares coral to trees but never claims it grows faster.

choices.text: Warm water is the only factor that determines how thick a coral band grows.
choices.rationale: Chemistry and season both matter; warmth is not called the only factor.

choices.text: Researchers prefer studying coral because it is easier than studying trees.
choices.rationale: No claim of relative ease over tree study is made.

choices.text: Coral bands preserve a long, readable record of past ocean conditions.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage centers on how coral bands record and reveal past conditions.

questions.explanation: The passage frames the coral as a centuries-long record that researchers learn to read.

stimulus.title: The Coral That Keeps Time
stimulus.text: A coral skeleton grows in fine bands, much like the rings of a tree. In bright, warm months the coral lays down thick layers; in cooler, dimmer months the layers thin. By slicing a coral and counting these bands, researchers can read a record of past seasons stretching back centuries. Even better, the chemistry trapped in each band hints at the water's temperature when it formed. So a single old coral can serve as a kind of diary, written not in words but in stone, recording conditions long before anyone thought to measure them. The challenge is learning to read a language no one designed to be read.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Plants are able to uproot themselves and walk to find better ground.
choices.rationale: The passage opens by noting a plant cannot walk.

choices.text: Plants have evolved varied methods to disperse their seeds away from the parent.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage surveys several strategies plants use to move their seeds.

choices.text: Wind is the only means by which any plant can spread its seeds.
choices.rationale: The passage describes wind, hooks, and fruit, not wind alone.

choices.text: Seeds always grow best directly beneath the shade of the parent plant.
choices.rationale: The passage says seeds need to leave the parent's shadow.

questions.explanation: The passage's focus is the variety of seed-dispersal strategies.

stimulus.title: Travelers Without Legs
stimulus.text: A plant cannot walk, yet its seeds must somehow leave the shadow of the parent and find open ground. Evolution has answered this need with a surprising range of tricks. Some seeds grow papery wings and spin away on the wind like tiny helicopters. Others wear hooks that snag the fur of passing animals, hitching a ride for miles. Still others hide inside sweet fruit, counting on an animal to eat them and carry them off, depositing them far away. Each method is a kind of bargain struck with the world around the plant. The seed that travels farthest is often the one with the best chance to grow where the parent's shade cannot reach.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Reformers opposed the printed ballot as an unnecessary change.
choices.rationale: Reformers pushed for the printed ballot, not against it.

choices.text: Public voting by show of hands gave ordinary workers the most power.
choices.rationale: Public voting invited pressure on workers, reducing their power.

choices.text: Voting has always been conducted privately, in every place and period of recorded history.
choices.rationale: The passage says voting was long public, not always private.

choices.text: The secret ballot freed voters to choose without fear of pressure or retaliation.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how private ballots protected voters from pressure.

questions.explanation: The passage's point is that the secret ballot protected the ordinary voter's free choice.

stimulus.title: The Secret Ballot
stimulus.text: It is easy to assume voting has always been private, but for a long time it was not. In many places people voted aloud or by a show of hands, in full view of employers, landlords, and neighbors. That openness invited pressure: a worker might think twice before voting against a boss who could see the choice. Reformers pushed for a printed ballot, marked alone and dropped in a box, so that no one need fear retaliation for an honest vote. The change seemed minor, a mere matter of paper, yet it shifted real power toward the ordinary voter, who could now decide without an audience.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Locks required rare and costly materials that few towns could ever afford.
choices.rationale: The passage stresses humble means, not rare materials.

choices.text: Canal locks let boats overcome changes in elevation, opening inland trade.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how locks conquer elevation and thereby expand trade.

choices.text: Boats could always travel freely inland long before the lock was invented.
choices.rationale: The passage says elevation once blocked inland travel.

choices.text: Rivers were once the fastest possible way to move goods over long distances.
choices.rationale: The passage does not rank rivers as the fastest route.

questions.explanation: The lock's purpose and its effect on inland commerce are the passage's focus.

stimulus.title: Stairs for Boats
stimulus.text: Rivers do not run level, and for centuries that simple fact blocked boats from traveling far inland. The lock changed things. A lock is a chamber with gates at each end; a boat enters, the gates close, and water is let in or drained out until the boat rises or falls to the next stretch of river. String several locks together, and a vessel can climb a hillside the way a person climbs a staircase. The engineering is humble, relying on nothing more exotic than gravity and patience, yet it knit distant towns into trading partners and turned shallow rivers into highways of commerce.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Mr. Owusu's attentiveness to customers, not his produce, made his stall special.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage stresses that customers returned because he knew and remembered them.

choices.text: Mr. Owusu succeeded mainly because his vegetables cost less than his rivals' did.
choices.rationale: The passage says it was not his prices that set him apart.

choices.text: Mr. Owusu's daughter took over the stall and ran it just as he had.
choices.rationale: The daughter notices his gift; the passage does not say she took over.

choices.text: The market declined because several stalls closed at around the same time.
choices.rationale: The passage notes that not a single other stall had closed.

questions.explanation: The passage's point is that personal attentiveness, not produce, drew customers back.

stimulus.title: The Stall That Listened
stimulus.text: Every Saturday, Mr. Owusu set out the same vegetables on the same table, and for years his stall was just one among many. What set him apart, his daughter noticed, was not his prices but his memory. He recalled which customer's child disliked onions, who was cooking for a crowd that weekend, who had been ill and needed something gentle. He would set aside a perfect tomato for one regular and toss an extra handful of beans to another. People did not return only for the produce; they returned because, at his stall, they were known. When he finally retired, the market felt larger and lonelier, though not a single other stall had closed.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: The high cost of distant spices spurred voyages that eventually made spices common.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage links costly, rare spices to voyages that made them ordinary.

choices.text: Black pepper has always been a cheap and easily available kitchen ingredient.
choices.rationale: The passage says spices were once nearly as valuable as silver.

choices.text: Sailors avoided long voyages because the spice trade was already too crowded.
choices.rationale: The high prices drove sailors to seek new routes, not avoid voyages.

choices.text: European merchants invented spices and were the first ever to harvest them.
choices.rationale: Merchants traded spices; they did not invent or first harvest them.

questions.explanation: The passage traces spices from costly rarity to abundance through new sea routes.

stimulus.title: The Price of Pepper
stimulus.text: There was a time when a handful of black pepper could rival a handful of silver. The spice grew only in distant lands, and by the time it reached a European market it had passed through many hands, each adding a markup. Merchants guarded their routes jealously and spread tall tales about how spices were harvested, partly to discourage rivals. The high prices drove sailors to seek their own sea paths to the source, voyages that redrew the map of the world. In the end, the very abundance those voyages produced made spices ordinary, and the fortunes built on rarity quietly dissolved.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Mosses and small plants arrive on bare rock before any lichen does.
choices.rationale: The passage says lichens come first and mosses follow.

choices.text: Lichens compete with one another for the limited sunlight on a rock.
choices.rationale: Competition among lichens is not the focus.

choices.text: Lichens are the only living things able to survive on exposed rock surfaces.
choices.rationale: The passage does not claim lichens are the only rock survivors.

choices.text: Lichens prepare bare rock for later plants by helping form the first soil.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage shows lichens building the soil that lets later plants grow.

questions.explanation: The passage frames the lichen as a pioneer that makes soil for what comes next.

stimulus.title: First on the Rock
stimulus.text: When a bare rock is left exposed, the first life to arrive is often a lichen, a strange partnership of fungus and alga living as one. The fungus grips the stone and gathers moisture; the alga, sheltered inside, makes food from sunlight. Together they need no soil at all. As a lichen grows, it slowly releases acids that crack the rock surface, and its dead tissue mixes with grit to form the first thin crumbs of soil. Years later, mosses and small plants can take root in that beginning. The lichen will likely be crowded out by the very community it made possible, an unsung founder of the green world that follows.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Gutenberg's reusable metal type made books far easier to reproduce and to spread.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage emphasizes how reusable type transformed the reproduction and reach of books.

choices.text: The price of books dropped instantly once Gutenberg's printing press appeared.
choices.rationale: The passage explicitly says costs did not fall overnight.

choices.text: Handwritten books remained more beautiful and more highly valued than any printed book.
choices.rationale: Beauty of handwriting is not the passage's claim.

choices.text: Scribes abandoned their work as soon as the first printing presses were built.
choices.rationale: It notes scholars still prized handwritten volumes, so scribes did not vanish at once.

questions.explanation: The passage frames the press as a turning point in how widely texts could circulate.

stimulus.title: Letters of Lead
stimulus.text: Before the 1450s, a book in Europe was copied by hand, a task that could occupy a scribe for a year. Johannes Gutenberg changed that arithmetic. By casting individual letters in metal, he could arrange them into a page, print hundreds of copies, then rearrange the same letters for the next page. The cost of a book did not fall overnight, and many scholars still prized handwritten volumes. But within fifty years, presses across the continent had produced millions of books. Ideas that once crept from city to city now traveled in bulk, and a reader in one town could hold the exact words read by a stranger far away.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Farming is effectively impossible anywhere within reach of a volcano.
choices.rationale: The passage says many people do farm there.

choices.text: Potassium is the single mineral that crops need in order to grow well.
choices.rationale: It names potassium and phosphorus, not a single required mineral.

choices.text: Volcanic ash builds fertile soil, drawing farmers despite the danger of eruptions.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains the fertility-versus-danger trade-off that keeps farmers near volcanoes.

choices.text: Volcanoes pose essentially no danger to the farms and villages that sit on their slopes.
choices.rationale: The passage notes a real danger, so volcanoes are not harmless.

questions.explanation: The passage balances the benefit of fertile soil against eruption risk.

stimulus.title: Gifts of the Volcano
stimulus.text: It seems strange that people would farm in the shadow of a volcano, but many do, and for good reason. When a volcano erupts, it scatters ash rich in minerals such as potassium and phosphorus. Over years, this ash breaks down into some of the most fertile soil on Earth. Crops planted in it can grow unusually well, which is why slopes near certain volcanoes are crowded with farms and villages. The bargain is uneasy: the same mountain that feeds the fields can also threaten them. Farmers weigh the steady gift of rich soil against the rare but real danger overhead, and generation after generation, many choose to stay.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: The tardigrade endures extreme conditions by drying into a protected, revivable state.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage centers on how the tardigrade endures extremes by drying out.

choices.text: The tardigrade is the smallest animal that scientists have ever discovered anywhere on Earth.
choices.rationale: The passage compares its size to salt but never calls it the smallest animal.

choices.text: The tardigrade can survive only in the vacuum and radiation of outer space.
choices.rationale: Space is one extreme it can survive, not its home.

choices.text: Scientists have now fully explained exactly how the tardigrade protects its cells.
choices.rationale: The text says scientists are 'still untangling' the mechanism.

questions.explanation: The passage's focus is the dehydration survival strategy and its partial explanation.

stimulus.title: The Survivor
stimulus.text: Smaller than a grain of salt, the tardigrade looks almost comical, plodding on eight stubby legs. Its talent, however, is anything but ordinary. When its surroundings dry out, the creature expels most of its water and curls into a husk called a tun. In this state it can endure boiling heat, the vacuum of space, and doses of radiation that would kill nearly any other animal. Years later, a single drop of water can revive it. Scientists are still untangling how the tardigrade protects its cells, but one clue is a special set of proteins that seem to harden into glass, cradling delicate structures until water returns.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Sparrows learn local song dialects that vary by place and shift across generations.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains learned, place-based dialects that change over generations.

choices.text: Human accents are largely caused by people imitating nearby birdsong.
choices.rationale: The human-accent comparison is an analogy, not a cause.

choices.text: Every white-crowned sparrow sings exactly the same unchanging song wherever it lives.
choices.rationale: The passage stresses variation, not sameness.

choices.text: Sparrows are born already knowing the full song they will sing as adults.
choices.rationale: Birds must learn the song; they are not born knowing it.

questions.explanation: The passage's through-line is learned, drifting song dialects.

stimulus.title: Songs With Accents
stimulus.text: A white-crowned sparrow raised near San Francisco does not sing quite like one raised a hundred miles north. The basic melody is the same, but small flourishes differ from place to place, forming what biologists call song dialects. Young sparrows learn these dialects by listening to adult males during a brief window in their first months. A bird that hears no song in that window grows up to sing a thin, simplified tune. The dialects can drift over generations, much as human accents do, so a recording made decades ago may sound subtly foreign to the birds singing in the same meadow today.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Treating zero as a true number transformed how people could write and calculate.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage shows how recognizing zero as a number reshaped writing and calculation.

choices.text: Mathematicians decided that zero should be removed entirely from written calculations.
choices.rationale: Mathematicians embraced zero, rather than removing it.

choices.text: Zero was always understood as an ordinary number throughout all of history.
choices.rationale: The passage says zero was long absent and unsettling, not always understood.

choices.text: Ancient people were unable to count sheep or coins without using zero.
choices.rationale: The passage says people counted sheep and coins easily without zero.

questions.explanation: The passage's point is that accepting zero as a number transformed mathematics.

stimulus.title: The Number That Was Nothing
stimulus.text: For much of history, there was no symbol for nothing. People counted sheep and coins easily enough, but the idea of writing down an empty amount seemed pointless, even unsettling. The breakthrough came when mathematicians treated zero not as the absence of a number but as a number in its own right, one that could be added, subtracted, and used to hold a place in larger figures. With zero, the difference between 5 and 50 could be written clearly, and long calculations grew far simpler. A concept that once felt like a riddle became the quiet hinge on which much of modern mathematics turns.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Plastic disappears completely and harmlessly once sunlight has acted on it.
choices.rationale: It says plastic fragments rather than vanishes.

choices.text: Microplastics can be filtered out of the open ocean cheaply and quite easily.
choices.rationale: The passage says filtering is nearly impossible.

choices.text: Scientists have firmly proven that microplastics pose no danger whatsoever to human health.
choices.rationale: It says health effects are not yet clear.

choices.text: Plastic breaks into tiny, far-spread particles that resist removal, so prevention is best.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage describes the spread and persistence of microplastics and favors prevention.

questions.explanation: The passage links persistence and spread to a prevention-first conclusion.

stimulus.title: Small Pieces, Wide Reach
stimulus.text: Plastic does not simply vanish. Exposed to sunlight and waves, a bottle or bag breaks into ever-smaller fragments until the pieces are too tiny to see. These microplastics have turned up in river water, in Arctic ice, and even in the bodies of fish and birds. Because the particles are so small, filtering them out of the ocean is nearly impossible. Researchers caution that the full effects on health are not yet clear, and they warn against easy conclusions. What is clear is that the cheapest fix is also the simplest: keeping plastic out of the environment in the first place, before it can shatter into pieces no net can catch.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: A delta is built by river sediment and shrinks when that supply is cut off.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains deltas as sediment-built land that erodes when the supply is trapped.

choices.text: Deltas are permanent landforms that never change once they have formed.
choices.rationale: The passage stresses deltas are a constantly rebuilt balance, not permanent.

choices.text: Rivers carry only clear water and never any soil from distant hills.
choices.rationale: The passage says rivers carry soil, not only water.

choices.text: Dams reliably help deltas grow larger by holding back excess water.
choices.rationale: Dams starve deltas by trapping sediment, not helping them grow.

questions.explanation: The passage shows deltas as sediment-dependent land that retreats when starved of mud.

stimulus.title: Land Made of Mud
stimulus.text: A great river carries more than water; it carries soil, scoured from distant hills and ground into fine particles. Where the river finally slows and meets the sea, it can no longer hold this load, and the sediment settles out, building flat new land called a delta. Over centuries a delta can grow seaward, fanning into a maze of channels and islands. But the process depends on a steady supply of mud. When dams upstream trap that sediment, the delta is starved; waves carry off more land than the river replaces, and the coastline begins to retreat. What looks like permanent ground is, in truth, a balance constantly being rebuilt.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Railroads drove the shift from local sun time to shared, standardized time zones.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how railway schedules forced a move to shared time zones.

choices.text: Standard time zones existed long before any railroads were ever built.
choices.rationale: Time zones came in response to railroads, not before them.

choices.text: People universally welcomed standard time the moment it was first proposed.
choices.rationale: The passage says people grumbled at first before accepting the change.

choices.text: Towns before railroads all happened to keep exactly the same time as one another by chance.
choices.rationale: The passage says each town kept its own time, not the same time.

questions.explanation: The passage's point is that railroads pushed local time into standardized zones.

stimulus.title: When Noon Moved
stimulus.text: Before railroads, every town kept its own time, set by the sun overhead at noon. A traveler crossing the country adjusted a watch town by town, and no one minded a few minutes' difference. Railroads made the patchwork intolerable. Trains ran on schedules, and a schedule means nothing if each station defines noon differently; a missed connection could be a matter of life and death. So the railways carved the land into broad zones, each agreeing to share a single time. People grumbled at first about clocks that no longer matched the sun, but the convenience won out. The hour on the wall had become a public agreement rather than a private reading of the sky.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: The very first bicycle was an immediate and widely celebrated success with the public.
choices.rationale: The first version was mocked and faded, not an immediate success.

choices.text: The bicycle evolved through gradual improvements into a popular means of free travel.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage traces stepwise improvements leading to the bicycle's popularity and freedom of movement.

choices.text: Working foot pedals were a built-in part of the very first bicycle design.
choices.rationale: The earliest version had no pedals.

choices.text: Early bicycles still depended on a horse in order to move from place to place.
choices.rationale: The passage says it needed no horse.

questions.explanation: The passage's arc is incremental improvement culminating in widespread, independent travel.

stimulus.title: The Machine That Walked
stimulus.text: The earliest ancestor of the bicycle had no pedals at all. Built in 1817, it was a wooden frame on two wheels that a rider straddled and pushed along with the feet, like walking while seated. People mocked it, and rutted roads made it impractical, so it soon faded. Decades passed before inventors added pedals, then a chain, then air-filled tires that smoothed the ride. Each change drew new riders, and by the 1890s the bicycle had become a craze. It offered something rare for the time: cheap, independent travel that needed no horse and no rails. For many people, especially those long denied easy movement, the machine quietly widened the boundaries of daily life.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: The library was destroyed in a single, well-documented, and sudden great fire.
choices.rationale: The passage says the single-fire story oversimplifies a slow decline.

choices.text: The library, as a matter of policy, refused to copy any scroll brought to it.
choices.rationale: The library actively copied scrolls.

choices.text: The library pursued a sweeping goal of universal knowledge whose ideal outlived it.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage stresses the ambition of universal collection and the lasting power of that idea.

choices.text: Only scholars who lived in the city itself were ever allowed to use the library's scrolls.
choices.rationale: Scholars came from distant lands.

questions.explanation: The passage's emphasis is the ambitious ideal and its endurance, not a single dramatic end.

stimulus.title: A House for Every Book
stimulus.text: The ancient library at Alexandria aimed at something audacious: to gather a copy of every book in the world. Ships docking at the harbor were searched, and any scrolls aboard were copied; sometimes the library kept the original and returned the copy. Scholars from distant lands came to read, argue, and write, and the collection may have held hundreds of thousands of scrolls. We know less than we would like about how the library declined, and popular stories of a single great fire oversimplify a slow loss across centuries. Still, the idea behind it endured. The dream of one place that holds all knowledge has reappeared, in new forms, ever since.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Modern forecasting completely discarded every part of the older tradition of weather watching.
choices.rationale: The passage says modern forecasting absorbed, not discarded, the best parts.

choices.text: Folk weather knowledge was entirely accurate and never mistaken in any case.
choices.rationale: The passage says much folk knowledge was unreliable.

choices.text: Folk weather signs mixed superstition with genuine insight that modern forecasting absorbed.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says folk signs blended superstition and real wisdom, the best of which forecasting absorbed.

choices.text: Farmers ignored the sky and the land when trying to predict the weather.
choices.rationale: The passage shows farmers read the sky and land closely.

questions.explanation: The passage balances the flaws and genuine insight of folk weather signs.

stimulus.title: Reading the Weather Before Radio
stimulus.text: Long before satellites mapped storms from orbit, farmers learned to read the sky and the land for signs of coming weather. A ring of haze around the moon, the smell of soil before rain, the behavior of swallows flying low: such clues were gathered into almanacs and passed down through families. Much of this folk knowledge was unreliable, mixing keen observation with superstition. Yet some of it held real wisdom, since the conditions that produce a hazy moon truly can precede rain. Modern forecasting has not so much replaced this older watching as absorbed its best parts, trading the rooster's crow for the radar's sweep.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the text is to

choices.text: describe the technical steps involved in baking a loaf of bread from scratch
choices.rationale: Only a few steps are mentioned, and they serve the story rather than instruct.

choices.text: explain why the narrator eventually chose a career as a professional baker
choices.rationale: Nothing indicates the narrator became a baker.

choices.text: recount how a brief remark from a mentor taught the narrator a lesson about patience
choices.rationale: Correct. The text builds to Mrs. Delgado's remark and the narrator's lasting lesson about not rushing.

choices.text: argue that practical summer jobs teach adolescents far more than formal schooling ever can
choices.rationale: The narrator compares the remark favorably with school but makes no general argument about jobs.

questions.explanation: The narrative exists to deliver the lesson 'Bread is not' in a hurry and its effect on the narrator.

stimulus.title: Proof
stimulus.text: The summer I was sixteen, I worked the four a.m. shift at Delgado's, mostly because nobody else would. Mrs. Delgado did not believe in teaching; she believed in watching. For two weeks I shaped loaves beside her while she said nothing, and for two weeks my loaves came out of the oven squat and sullen, like they resented being made. Then one morning she pressed a finger into my dough, frowned, and said, 'You are in a hurry. Bread is not.' That was all. I slowed down. I let the dough rest in the proof box until it had nearly doubled, instead of until I got bored. The loaf that came out that day was not perfect, but it rose. I have thought about that sentence more often than anything I learned in school, mostly when I am about to rush something that will not be rushed.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Sleep is an active process that supports memory and brain upkeep, in the right amount.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage presents sleep as active and beneficial within an optimal range.

choices.text: The brain does essentially nothing of value during the hours a person sleeps.
choices.rationale: The passage argues the brain is busy during sleep.

choices.text: Staying awake for longer stretches reliably improves a person's memory of new material.
choices.rationale: The experiment shows the opposite of this claim.

choices.text: The more hours a person sleeps each night, the better that person performs.
choices.rationale: The passage explicitly rejects 'more is always better.'

questions.explanation: The passage's balanced claim is that sleep actively helps the brain, but only in adequate amounts.

stimulus.title: The Night Shift of the Brain
stimulus.text: Sleep can look like idleness, but the brain is busy. During deep sleep, waves of electrical activity sweep across the cortex, and researchers think these waves help move the day's memories into longer-term storage. In one line of experiments, students who slept after studying a list of words remembered more of them than students who stayed awake the same number of hours. Sleep may also clear away molecular waste that builds up while we are awake. None of this means more sleep is always better; the relationship appears to follow a curve, with both too little and too much linked to poorer performance. What the brain seems to need is enough, at the right times.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Drilling into ice destroys the trapped bubbles before they can be studied.
choices.rationale: The passage describes analyzing the bubbles, not destroying them.

choices.text: Polar snow melts completely each summer before the next winter's snowfall.
choices.rationale: The passage says winter snow does not entirely melt.

choices.text: Ice cores are useful only for measuring the present-day composition of air.
choices.rationale: Cores let researchers study ancient, not just present, air.

choices.text: Ice cores preserve ancient air in layered bubbles that record past atmospheres.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how layered ice traps and dates ancient air.

questions.explanation: The passage centers on ice cores as a layered record of past atmospheres.

stimulus.title: Bubbles of Old Air
stimulus.text: Each winter's snowfall on a polar ice sheet does not entirely melt; it packs down, traps tiny pockets of air, and slowly turns to ice. Layer settles on layer, year after year, so that drilling deep into the ice is a way of drilling back through time. Trapped in those bubbles is a sample of the very atmosphere that existed when the snow fell, including the gases it carried. By analyzing cores pulled from kilometers down, researchers can compare today's air with the air of tens of thousands of years ago. The ice keeps no diary of dates, yet its layers, counted carefully, let scientists assign an age to each whisper of ancient air.

questions.prompt: Which choice best describes what happens in the text?

choices.text: A chess player loses her knight through carelessness and realizes too late that the game is lost.
choices.rationale: The knight is given up deliberately, as part of a plan.

choices.text: A chess coach interrupts a tournament match to advise his student on managing her remaining time.
choices.rationale: The coach's voice is remembered, not present.

choices.text: Two chess players agree to a draw after both run short of time in a long and evenly matched game.
choices.rationale: No draw occurs.

choices.text: Under time pressure, a chess player narrows her focus and commits to a sacrifice that unsettles her opponent.
choices.rationale: Correct. Priya applies her coach's advice, finds a path requiring the knight, and the boy finally looks up.

questions.explanation: The scene turns on Priya's focused decision and its effect on her opponent.

stimulus.title: Forty Moves
stimulus.text: By the thirtieth move, Priya had stopped seeing the pieces as pieces. The knight on the rim was a trapped thing with one way out; the pawn on the sixth rank was a promise she had made twenty moves earlier and now had to keep. Across the table her opponent, a boy in a sweatshirt who had not looked up once, took her bishop with an unhurried hand and pressed the clock. Nine minutes left for her, fourteen for him. Her coach's voice surfaced: when you are behind on time, do not think faster; think about fewer things. She let the whole board blur except for the pawn and the two squares in front of it. There was a path. It required giving up the knight, which her hand did not want to do, and she noticed, with something like amusement, that her hand had opinions. She moved the knight anyway. The boy looked up.

questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall impression the letter conveys?

choices.text: The writer believes the captain deceived the travelers and intends to expose his dishonesty.
choices.rationale: He treats the captain's lateness wryly, not as deception to be exposed.

choices.text: The writer regrets leaving home and plans to return to his family as soon as he possibly can.
choices.rationale: He expresses no plan to return.

choices.text: The writer is thrilled by the beauty of the landscape and eager for his family to join him there soon.
choices.rationale: He says the country is 'nothing like the engravings' and describes it unflatteringly.

choices.text: The writer is disappointed by the camp but finds small compensations in the experience.
choices.rationale: Correct. Thomas catalogs disappointments but values the lesson about finding water.

questions.explanation: The letter balances complaint with a note of something gained.

stimulus.title: A Letter from the Camp
stimulus.text: Dear Margaret, You will forgive the hand; I am writing on the lid of a trunk by the light of a lamp that smokes. We reached the river camp on Tuesday, two days later than the captain promised and a full week later than Father feared, which puts the truth, as usual, somewhere between hope and worry. The country here is nothing like the engravings. The hills are brown and lie about in heaps, and the river is the color of weak coffee. I had expected to be lonely and find instead that I am never alone, which is worse. There are forty of us in a space meant for twenty. Still, this morning a boy no older than you showed me how to find water by watching where the birds go at dusk, and I thought: here is something I would not have learned at home. Tell Mother I am eating. It is nearly true. Your brother, Thomas.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Ines has grown so skilled at tending the lamp that she now keeps the log far more carefully than her father ever did.
choices.rationale: Her script is described as 'looser' than her father's careful hand, so she is not more careful than he was.

choices.text: Ines takes over her ill father's duties and finds meaning in the beam's silent message to distant sailors.
choices.rationale: Correct. The text follows Ines doing her father's work and locates her feeling in the beam reaching unseen sailors.

choices.text: Ines resents the lighthouse and performs her father's duties only because no one else in the family is willing.
choices.rationale: The text says she does not love the lighthouse 'exactly,' but it describes attachment, not resentment, and no other family members appear.

choices.text: Ines dreams of leaving the lighthouse so that she can finally speak with the sailors whose ships pass at night.
choices.rationale: She values the imagined contact with sailors; nothing suggests she wants to leave.

questions.explanation: The passage centers on Ines's quiet stewardship of the light and the one-word 'conversation' it lets her have.

stimulus.title: The Lamp Room
stimulus.text: Every evening at dusk, Ines climbed the one hundred and twelve iron steps to the lamp room, counting them under her breath as her father had taught her. He was ill that winter, and the keeper's log, which he had kept in his cramped, careful hand for twenty years, now bore her looser script. She trimmed the wick, polished the great lens until her own face swam in it, and set the clockwork turning. Below, the sea worried at the rocks. Ines did not love the lighthouse, exactly; she loved the moment when the beam first swung out across the water and she imagined a ship's mate, miles off, lifting his head. It was the only conversation she had ever had with strangers, and it consisted of a single word, repeated all night: here.

questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the text's central concern?

choices.text: A woman has decided to leave her family permanently in order to pursue a career in music.
choices.rationale: She 'had not yet decided whether she would get on.'

choices.text: A woman is annoyed that her town has never bothered to repair the station's unreliable clock.
choices.rationale: The clock is atmosphere, not her concern.

choices.text: A woman is traveling to the city to care for an ailing cousin for a period of two weeks.
choices.rationale: The cousin is a cover story; 'the fortnight did not' exist.

choices.text: A woman stands between the life she has and an opportunity she had set aside.
choices.rationale: Correct. The letter from her past and her indecision on the platform frame the choice.

questions.explanation: The scene is a woman poised between two lives.

stimulus.title: The Eleven-Forty
stimulus.text: The station at Harwell had two platforms and one clock, and the clock was wrong, which everyone in town knew and no one corrected. Mrs. Abernathy stood under it in her good coat with a hatbox at her feet. She had told her sister she was going to visit a cousin in the city for a fortnight. The cousin existed; the fortnight did not. In her handbag, beneath the gloves, was a letter from a music conservatory addressed to a Miss E. Abernathy, which she had not been for twelve years, and which she had opened at the kitchen table that morning while the kettle screamed and nobody came to take it off. The eleven-forty was late. It was always late, by exactly the amount the clock was wrong, so that it arrived, in a manner of speaking, on time. She picked up the hatbox when she heard it. She had not yet decided whether she would get on.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the author's main argument?

choices.text: Tracking habits and optimizing schedules are the most effective ways of solving stubborn intellectual problems quickly.
choices.rationale: The author says problems come loose away from the desk.

choices.text: Rest should be understood primarily as an investment that yields returns in the quality of later work.
choices.rationale: This is the view the author criticizes.

choices.text: Unstructured time is valuable in itself and is also the condition for the insight that productivity culture wants.
choices.rationale: Correct. The author defends time 'not for anything' and notes that insight comes from it anyway.

choices.text: People should work fewer hours so that they have more time to rest and recover from their demanding jobs.
choices.rationale: The author says 'I do not propose that anyone work less.'

questions.explanation: Idle time is defended both for its own sake and for what it yields.

stimulus.title: In Defense of Doing Nothing
stimulus.text: We have made an idol of productivity. Every hour is to be optimized, every habit tracked, every pause justified as 'recharging' for the work to come. Even rest is permitted only as an investment. I want to argue for something less respectable: time that is not for anything. The case is not sentimental. Most people can name the moment a stubborn problem came loose, and it was rarely at the desk. It was in the shower, on a walk, in the dull middle of a long drive. The mind does its deepest sorting when it is left alone, and it cannot be left alone on a schedule. A culture that fills every gap does not merely tire its members; it starves the very faculty it claims to prize. I do not propose that anyone work less. I propose that when the work is done, we stop pretending that the hours afterward owe us a return. Some of them will pay anyway. That is not why they are worth having.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The narrator came to believe that a map with gaps is useless to sailors and should never be issued by the Admiralty.
choices.rationale: The narrator values gaps, not rejects them.

choices.text: A northern voyage failed to survey a stretch of coast because of nine days of fog, forcing the Admiralty to send a second expedition.
choices.rationale: No second expedition is mentioned; the fog is the occasion, not the subject.

choices.text: The narrator's master was so cautious in his work that he failed to complete most of the charts the Admiralty had commissioned from him.
choices.rationale: Nothing suggests Hallam failed to complete charts.

choices.text: A mapmaker's refusal to invent a coastline taught the narrator that honesty about ignorance outweighs a finished look.
choices.rationale: Correct. Hallam leaves the gap, and the narrator comes to see gaps as 'the most honest lines.'

questions.explanation: Honesty about what is unknown is the lesson.

stimulus.title: The Unfinished Coast
stimulus.text: My master, Mr. Hallam, had drawn maps for the Admiralty for thirty years, and in all that time, he told me, he had never once drawn a line he had not been given reason to believe. I was nineteen and thought this a modest ambition. It was my task that winter to copy the surveys sent back from the northern voyage, and I came to a stretch of coast where the ship's log simply stopped: fog for nine days, then open sea. The chart before me showed a gap. I proposed to close it with a gentle curve, as any sensible coast would run. Mr. Hallam took the pen from my hand. 'A sailor who trusts that curve,' he said, 'will put his ship on rocks we have not seen, and he will do it in the dark, and he will do it because you were tidy.' He left the gap. I have since drawn a great many maps, and some of them have gaps, and I have come to think of the gaps as the most honest lines on them.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Judging oneself by the moods of colleagues and the outcomes of distant events is a sign of unusual conscientiousness.
choices.rationale: The author presents this habit as a mistake, not a virtue.

choices.text: Keeping a written record of weekly failures is the most reliable way to become wiser over the course of a lifetime.
choices.rationale: The original list made the author miserable, not wiser.

choices.text: Separating what one controls from what one does not makes self-assessment more honest and less painful.
choices.rationale: Correct. The author adopts the philosophers' line and finds the resulting list truer and more bearable.

choices.text: The ancient philosophers were wrong to claim that events outside our control are of little importance to our lives.
choices.rationale: The text says the philosophers did not call external events unimportant.

questions.explanation: The essay's arc is from a self-punishing list to one limited to what is 'ours.'

stimulus.title: What Is Ours
stimulus.text: I used to keep a list of things that had gone wrong that week, with the idea that reviewing it would make me wiser. It made me miserable instead, and I eventually understood why. Most of the items were not mine. The weather, a colleague's mood, the outcome of a vote in a city I had never visited: I had been grading myself on events in which I had no vote. An ancient school of philosophers drew a line that I have since found useful. On one side are the things within our power—our judgments, our efforts, our intentions. On the other side is everything else. They did not say that the second category is unimportant, only that it is not ours, and that confusing the two is the chief source of unhappiness. I still keep a list. It is shorter now, and every item on it is something I actually did, or failed to do. On bad weeks it is a harder list to read. On good weeks it is the only one that counts.

questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the central concern of the text?

choices.text: Two siblings discover, while dividing their mother's belongings, that their attachments are stronger than they had admitted.
choices.rationale: Correct. Ben's 'No,' said 'too quickly,' exposes an attachment he had denied.

choices.text: A brother agrees to sell his mother's clock because he has never liked it and has no use for it in his own apartment.
choices.rationale: He refuses to sell it.

choices.text: Two siblings argue bitterly over a valuable clock, and the dispute reveals a long-standing rivalry between them that dates to childhood.
choices.rationale: There is no bitterness and no rivalry; the clock is one of the 'small things,' not a valuable item.

choices.text: Two siblings efficiently divide their mother's possessions by assigning each item to whichever of them has the better claim to it.
choices.rationale: The small things are exactly where easy division fails.

questions.explanation: Unacknowledged attachment surfacing is the heart of the scene.

stimulus.title: Division
stimulus.text: 'You take the clock,' Dana said. 'You always liked it.' 'I never liked it,' said Ben. 'I wound it because nobody else would.' They were sitting on the floor of their mother's apartment with the lists between them, hers typed, his on the back of an envelope. It was the fourth hour. They had agreed easily on the furniture, which neither wanted, and the photographs, which they would scan and share, and had come, as they had both known they would, to the small things: the clock, the chipped blue bowl, the cheap ring their mother had worn in place of the good one she kept in a drawer. 'Then I'll take it,' Dana said, and wrote it down, and Ben watched her write and felt, absurdly, that something had been taken from him. 'Or we could sell it,' she said, not looking up. 'No,' he said, too quickly, and they both heard it. She crossed it off her list. He picked up the clock. It was heavier than he remembered.

questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.rationale: The text says some towns refused; it never says they were forced.

choices.text: Most American towns before the 1880s kept their clocks carefully synchronized with the clocks of neighboring cities.
choices.rationale: Clocks differed from town to town, and nobody minded.

choices.text: The federal government imposed four time zones on the railroads in 1883 over the strong objections of the major rail companies.
choices.rationale: The rail companies created the zones; the government did not endorse them for thirty-five years.

questions.explanation: The passage is about how railroad time displaced local time through practice rather than law.

stimulus.title: Noon by Agreement
stimulus.text: Until the 1880s, noon in most American towns was simply the moment the sun stood highest over that town. A traveler heading west from one city to the next could find the clocks a few minutes behind at each stop, and nobody minded, because few people traveled fast enough to notice. The railroads changed this. A train running on a timetable built from dozens of local noons was a train waiting to collide with another. In 1883, the major rail companies divided the continent into four broad zones and declared that every clock within a zone would read the same. The federal government did not endorse the scheme for another thirty-five years, and some towns refused outright, keeping 'sun time' as a point of pride. But commerce followed the trains. Within a few years, most people had quietly agreed to let a company's timetable, rather than the sky, tell them what time it was.

stimulus.title: The Color of Thought
stimulus.text: An octopus has no bones and, oddly, almost no color of its own. Yet in less than a second it can flush deep red with alarm or fade to match the speckled gray of a stone. Beneath its skin lie millions of tiny sacs of pigment, each ringed by muscle. When the muscles pull, the sacs widen and color blooms; when they relax, the color vanishes. Stranger still, the octopus is colorblind, so it cannot see the very hues it produces. Some researchers suspect its skin itself senses light, letting the animal paint a disguise it can never admire.

questions.prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that a 'clean line' on a finished map represents

choices.text: a once-open question that exploration eventually answered
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says every clean line 'was once a question,' settled by explorers.

choices.text: a region that, even now, remains completely unknown
choices.rationale: Clean lines mark known, corrected regions.

choices.text: a mistake that no later mapmaker ever got around to correcting
choices.rationale: The line marks a settled answer, not an uncorrected mistake.

questions.explanation: A clean line stands for a once-open question now resolved.

stimulus.title: The Edge of the Map
stimulus.text: Old maps are full of guesses. Where knowledge ran out, mapmakers filled the blank spaces with mountains they had never seen and coastlines that bent the wrong way. Some added sea monsters, less from belief than from a need to decorate the unknown. As explorers returned with measurements, the guesses were slowly corrected, and the monsters swam off the page. But a finished, accurate map can hide how hard it was to make. Every clean line was once a question, settled only by someone willing to sail past the edge of what was known and come back with an answer.

questions.prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that the first version of the letter was

choices.text: an honest account of his deep homesickness
choices.rationale: The honest account was the second version, not the first.

questions.explanation: The first draft put on cheerfulness he did not truly feel.

stimulus.title: The Unsent Letter
stimulus.text: Tomas wrote the letter three times before he stopped trying to send it. In the first version he was cheerful, listing the small triumphs of his new city as if homesickness were a thing he had outgrown. In the second he was honest, and the page filled with everything he missed until it embarrassed him. The third version said almost nothing at all. He kept that one folded in a drawer. Months later he found it again and realized the words he could not send had still done their work: writing them had let him admit, if only to himself, how far from home he truly felt.

questions.prompt: The comparison to a fire extinguisher mainly suggests that the vault is

choices.text: useful for nothing other than literally putting out fires
choices.rationale: The analogy is about readiness, not literal firefighting.

questions.explanation: The analogy stresses preparedness for an uncommon emergency.

stimulus.title: A Vault for Seeds
stimulus.text: Deep inside a frozen mountain, a vault holds something more valuable than gold: seeds. Hundreds of thousands of varieties of crops, gathered from around the world, rest in sealed packets at temperatures far below freezing. The cold slows the seeds' aging to a crawl, so that even after decades they can still sprout. The vault is a backup. If a war, flood, or disease wipes out a crop somewhere, a sample can be withdrawn and grown again. Its keepers hope it will rarely be needed, the way one hopes never to use a fire extinguisher. Its value lies precisely in being ready and almost never used.

questions.prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that, before automation, a lighthouse's reliability depended on

choices.text: electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors doing the work
choices.rationale: Timers and sensors came later, with automation.

choices.text: the constant nightly labor of a dedicated human keeper
choices.rationale: Correct. Keepers performed the nightly tasks that kept the light burning.

choices.text: the complete absence of storms along that stretch of coast
choices.rationale: Storms occurred and made the work dangerous.

choices.text: the sheer height of the tower above the surrounding water
choices.rationale: Height alone did not keep the light lit.

questions.explanation: Reliability rested on the keeper's constant labor.

stimulus.title: Keeping the Light
stimulus.text: For centuries, a lighthouse meant a keeper. Someone had to climb the tower each night, trim the wick, polish the lens, and wind the clockwork that turned the light. Storms made the work dangerous, and isolation made it lonely, but ships depended on that faithful beam. In the twentieth century, automation arrived. Electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors took over the tasks one by one, and keepers were gradually withdrawn. The lights still shine, more reliably than ever, yet something human slipped away with the last keeper. The machines kept the promise of the light; they could not keep its company.

questions.prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that Nadia almost refused the loaner because she

choices.rationale: Correct. 'It felt wrong to play something so fine' signals a sense of unworthiness.

choices.text: actually preferred instruments whose tuning pegs kept slipping

choices.rationale: Nothing suggests she cannot read music.

choices.text: strongly disliked the pieces she was assigned for the recital
choices.rationale: Her feelings about the pieces are not the reason given.

questions.explanation: Her hesitation stems from feeling the instrument was too fine for her.

stimulus.title: The Borrowed Violin
stimulus.text: Nadia had practiced on a school instrument so battered that two of its pegs slipped during every lesson. When her teacher handed her a loaner violin for the recital, she nearly refused; it felt wrong to play something so fine. But as she drew the bow across the strings, the tone opened like a window onto a bright street. Notes she had fought for all year now arrived easily, as if the instrument had been waiting for her. Afterward, returning it to its case, she understood that her old struggles had not been wasted. The fine violin had simply revealed the player she had quietly become.

questions.prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that mixing glass colors during recycling

choices.rationale: Mixing clearly has a negative effect.

choices.text: reduces the usefulness, and so the value, of the recycled material
